summary: Two Boca Grande lights: an 1890 frame lighthouse at the Gasparilla Island tip, and an 1881 Delaware tower set up here in 1927 as the rear range light.

lens.where: The 1890 lantern later held a 375-377 mm drum lens (1986); the rear range tower was lit with a fourth-order Fresnel in 1932 and a replica fourth-order lens was unveiled in 2019

access.note: Port Boca Grande Lighthouse is in Gasparilla Island State Park, with a museum run by the Barrier Island Parks Society on set hours; the rear range tower opens to climbers on scheduled days only, and not in August. Do not climb outside scheduled tours.

facts.agency: State of Florida (owner); Barrier Island Parks Society (manages the museum and the rear range tower)

events.note: Congress appropriates $35,000 for a lighthouse at the southern tip of Gasparilla Island (LighthouseFriends)
Port Boca Grande lighthouse completed September 1890
Activated December 31, 1890
Third-and-a-half-order Fresnel, per the Board (1891) and the Digital Archive
Front beacon washed out by the shifting channel and re-erected on land, 175 ft from high-water mark and 475 ft from the main light
Contract for an oil house (Board report, entry 763)
Repairs completed September 30, 1899: slate roofs on keepers' dwellings; wharf extended to deep water
Characteristic changed March 23, 1900; original restored June 20, 1900
Keeper William Lester and assistant James T. Williams help save two power boats ashore near the station, May 19
Commissioner's report lists $7,607 for a sanitary plumbing system, concrete wharf and general repairs at the range station
Cape Henlopen (Delaware Breakwater Rear Range) tower reassembled on Gasparilla Island, painted white
Assistant keeper Charles F. Fine dies at the lighthouse on April 28 (LighthouseFriends gives the circumstances; not repeated in the story)
Rear range tower lit January 1, 1932 (fourth-order Fresnel)
Hurricane disturbance of July 28; the Jacksonville Weather Bureau calls reports from Gasparilla, among other lights, especially valuable
Lighthouse automated (LighthouseFriends)
The 1979 nomination says the light was moved two miles north in 1960; LighthouseFriends and the Digital Archive give 1966 for the end of service at the 1890 lighthouse (see notes_for_editor)
1890 lighthouse discontinued and abandoned by the Coast Guard; a 58-foot steel skeleton tower set up nearby
265-foot granite jetty built to protect the island and the lighthouse after erosion
Federal government transfers the lighthouse and about 13 acres to Lee County
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places
Re-commissioned as an active aid to navigation November 21, 1986, with a drum lens
Lighthouse and surrounding property transferred to the State of Florida; becomes Gasparilla Island State Park
Port Boca Grande lighthouse museum opens (LighthouseFriends: a decade after the 1989 BIPS formation)
Front range light of the Boca Grande entrance range discontinued
Hurricane Charley, August 13, destroys the catwalk and two cisterns
Coast Guard awards stewardship of the rear light to the Barrier Island Parks Society
Rear light deactivated in early 2017 (LighthouseFriends)
Rear range tower opens for climbing, first public climb in April 2017
Rear light relit February 9, 2019 as a private aid to navigation, with a replica fourth-order lens
Hurricane Ian damages the lighthouse; closed for repairs
Port Boca Grande lighthouse reopens in February 2024 after repairs

corrections.why: The record's coordinates are those of the 1932 rear range tower (LighthouseFriends ID 368 gives 26.74203, -82.26344). The name and 1890 date refer to the Port Boca Grande lighthouse, which LighthouseFriends (ID 369) places at 26.71735, -82.26091. The editor should decide whether the record should be split into the 1890 lighthouse and the rear range, and which point is the station's location.

corrections.proposed: 1927 reassembled on Gasparilla Island; 1932 first lit as rear range
corrections.why: The 1881 'built' date belongs to the Delaware Breakwater (Cape Henlopen) rear range tower, not the Boca Grande station. The tower was re-erected here in 1927 and lit in 1932.
The 1891 Board report gives the 1890 light's focal plane as 44 feet above mean low water (13.4 m). The rear range's 105-foot focal plane (LighthouseFriends ID 368) is about 32 m.

No source we read gives Oc W 4s. The 1891 Board report describes a fixed white light with a red flash every 20 seconds at the 1890 lighthouse, and LighthouseFriends gives the 2019 rear light as white, flashing every six seconds.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Both lights are lit according to the sources, which is why they seem to disagree. The 1890 Port Boca Grande lighthouse was re-commissioned as an active aid in 1986 (LighthouseFriends ID 369). The rear range was deactivated in early 2017 and relit as a private aid on February 9, 2019 (LighthouseFriends ID 368; Boca Beacon).

The 1891 Board report describes the 1890 light as a fixed white light with a red flash every 20 seconds. The rear range, relit in 2019, flashes white every six seconds (LighthouseFriends ID 368). Oc W 4s in the record has no source in our reading.

notes_for_editor: Sources disagree on the dates of the 1960 move (1979 NRHP nomination) and 1966 (LighthouseFriends and the Digital Archive). Railroad 1907 (LighthouseFriends) versus 1909 (NRHP). The 1890 lighthouse's current lens is a 375 mm drum (Digital Archive) or 377 mm (LighthouseFriends). The Digital Archive calls the 1890 lighthouse the 'Gasparilla Island Front Range', but the Light-House Board's 1899 entry calls it the 'rear' light, so that alias is unreliable. Wikipedia's Gasparilla Island Lights article (not cited) gives the Cape Henlopen tower's build year as 1885 and the rear light's decommissioning as 2014; LighthouseFriends and BIPS give 1881 and early 2017 and 2016 (stewardship), so the Cape Henlopen station's story should be checked. The record's characteristic 'Oc W 4s' and range of 12 nm have no source in our reading; the 1891 Board report gives the 1890 light as fixed white with red flash every 20 seconds, and the 2019 rear light flashes every six seconds (LighthouseFriends). A Light List check is needed. The 1888 appropriation rests on LighthouseFriends alone; the 1888-89 Board reports are not in our corpus. The USCG Historian's archived station page could not be read (the Wayback capture returned 404 for the paths tried). Chronicling America returned HTTP 520 for every search we tried (two queries), so no newspaper material is used. The 1916 Bulletin mention of Gasparilla is garbled in the OCR and was not used. The 'haunted' lore in LighthouseFriends was left out. The death of Charles F. Fine is given in one line, with the circumstances left to the source, for the editor's judgment. Keeper names are from the Digital Archive roster (NARA registers via the Kraig Anderson inventory); no individual keeper was confirmed against a primary register in this pass. The story counts 15 footnotes and 2 independent primary Board reports for the 1890 light. Fact-check 2026-10-22: the 1936 paragraph now follows the Bulletin (Florida reef light stations, plus lightships; Gasparilla is not a reef station). The 1891, 1892 and 1894 Board reports are cited by their fiscal years, and the 1899 repairs entry (scan p. 140) is footnote 15. The Port Boca Grande fill (1971-72) was pumped by Florida Power and Light, per LighthouseFriends. The 1979 nomination's 1960 'moved two miles to the north' is kept as the nomination's own date.
